0.value:
Gives the middle value of the values of an array that are actually there, skipping any that are nan (missing).

Real data has holes. A dropped frame, a sensor that lost tracking or a division by zero arrives as nan ("not a number"), and any arithmetic that touches a nan gives nan - so np.median of an array with a single nan in it is nan, which is correct and useless. np.nanmedian leaves the nan values out and works on the values that are actually there. The values present are sorted and the middle one taken (halfway between the two middle ones when the count is even), exactly as np.median does with a complete array.

WITH NO HOLES IT IS THE SAME:
If the array has no nan in it, np.nanmedian gives exactly what np.median gives. If EVERY value of the array (or of one column or row, along an axis) is nan there is nothing left to work on: the answer for it is nan, and numpy prints a RuntimeWarning in the console.

THE axis MENU:
With no axis (the default) the whole array is reduced to one number. With axis 0 the reduction runs DOWN each column, giving one result per column; with axis 1 it runs ALONG each row, giving one result per row. For a table of 5 frames (rows) of 4 sensors (columns), axis 0 answers "what did each sensor typically read", axis 1 "what did the sensors typically read at each frame". The axis named is the one that disappears: a 5 by 4 array gives 4 values on axis 0, 5 on axis 1. Along an axis the holes are skipped per column (or per row), so a column with one nan still gets a sensible answer from the others.

SYNTAX:
np.nanmedian <axis: int>
With no argument there is no axis: the whole array becomes one number.

EXAMPLE:
np.nanmedian 0

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

in:
The array (a list or a single number is turned into one). Every array that arrives is reduced and the result sent - the only inlet that makes the node send. A message such as 4.8 nan 5.0 makes a list with a nan in it: the word nan is read as the number.

axis (menu, also an inlet):
Which way to reduce - see THE axis MENU. Changing it does NOT send by itself; the next array uses it. The menu offers None (the whole array) and the axes the last array had (None and 0 for a 1-D array); a message None into the axis inlet also returns to the whole array. An axis the array does not have is treated as its last axis for that array only: the choice is kept, so one 1-D array through np.nanmedian 1 does not stop the 2-D arrays that follow from being reduced along axis 1.

OUTPUTS:

nanmedian:
With no axis, one number. With an axis, an array one dimension smaller: one result per column (axis 0) or per row (axis 1).

A MISSING READING (top demo):
Seven readings, one of them missing. Click the first message (with the nan): np.nanmedian gives the median of the six that are there, 4.95 (halfway between 4.9 and 5.0), and np.median gives nan. Click the second (the missing value filled in with 5.2) and the two agree on 5.0.

A LOST FRAME IN A TABLE (lower demo):
make_gap makes a 5 by 4 table - 5 frames of 4 sensors - and knocks out one cell (row 2, column 1) to nan; click the button for a new table. A heat_map has no colour for nan: find the cell labelled nan (row 2, column 1). Along axis 0 (one result per sensor), np.median gives nan for column 1 only - the other three columns are fine - while np.nanmedian gives column 1 the middle of its four remaining frames.

RELATED:
np.median is the same without the skipping. np.nanmean averages the values present; np.nansum adds them up. A median already ignores a few WRONG values - nanmedian also ignores MISSING ones, so it is the most forgiving of the lot. t.nanmedian is the PyTorch version.
